title: WPPIL/123/2017 of Dharmendra Singh Vs State Of Uttarakhand AND OTHERS

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT
NAINITAL
Writ Petition (PIL) No. 123 of 2017
Dharmendra Singh ...Petitioner
Vs.
State of Uttarakhand & others ...Respondents
Present:
Shri Gopal K. Verma, learned counsel for the petitioner.
Shri S.N. Babulkar, learned advocate general assisted by Shri Paresh
Tripathi, learned chief standing counsel for the State/respondent nos.1
to 6.
Shri H.M. Bhatia, learned counsel for respondent no. 7.
Shri Sandeep Tandon, learned counsel for respondent no. 8.
Shri Rakesh Thapliyal, learned senior counsel assisted by Shri Bhupesh
Kandpal, learned counsel for respondent nos. 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 16, 17,
18, 25, 26, 28, 29, 32, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 43, 44, 45, 46 & 47.
Shri B.P. Nautiyal, learned senior counsel assisted by Shri Mohd.
Matloob, learned counsel for respondent no. 15.
Shri Shashank Pandey, learned counsel for respondent nos. 13, 19, 27 &
31.
Shri Abhijay Negi, learned counsel for respondent nos. 33, 35, 42, 45 &
46.
Coram: Hon'ble Ravi Malimath, ACJ.
 Hon'ble N.S. Dhanik, J.
Hon'ble Ravi Malimath, ACJ. (Oral)
The petitioner claims to be a law abiding
citizen of India. That he is a resident of South Civil Line,
Roorkee, District Haridwar; that he is a social worker and
a RTI activist running a campaign against corruption in
various government departments and societies. He is
fighting for the rights of the people of the State.
2. It is his case that there is a huge tax evasion
and a heavy revenue loss by a syndicate of higher
officials of the Trade Tax (Revenue) Department of the
Uttarakhand Government. The same is with the collusion
of big industrialists, business houses, traders and
transporters. The rough estimate according to the

2
petitioner, from certain undisclosed sources of the State
Revenue Department, is an amount of more than ten
thousand crores every year which have been diverted by
the higher officials to their own pockets instead of adding
to the State Revenue. Therefore, the question raised by
the writ petitioner is as stated by him in para 4 of his
writ petition which reads as follows:
There is a question involved in the present writ
petition. Whether the money collected from the
Tax payers, industries, business houses,
traders, transporters by the official of the Trade
Tax Department should be deposited as State
Revenue or whether the syndicate of corrupt
higher official of the Trade Tax Department
may be kept free for tax evasion and allowed to
divert the public money in their own pockets by
adopting corrupt practice and built the Benami
properties in the name of their relatives."
3. It is pleaded in the petition that after creation
of the State of Uttarakhand several officials of a bad
reputation opted for the State of Uttarakhand and joined
the services of the State of Uttarakhand in the revenue
department; that they had taken full advantage of the
political imbalances and the lack of experience of the
political masters of the State of Uttarakhand; that the
political masters of the State being unknown to taxation
process did not interfere in the huge revenue losses
created by the syndicate of tax officers and businessmen;
that this syndicate took full advantage of the lawlessness,
greediness as well as the misbehavior of the political
masters etc. They started playing with free hands without
any fear of anybody and started filling up their pockets
by purchasing properties etc. He relies on a report dated
09.02.2009, vide annexure no. 1 to the writ petition,
which indicates the tax evasion by the BTC Industries,
etc. Various annexures have been produced to buttress
the arguments of the petitioner. The prayer sought for is
for a writ of mandamus to direct the constitution of a

3
High Level Committee under the supervision of the
Hon'ble High Court for an investigation into the huge
amount of tax evasion etc. A supplementary affidavit has
been filed annexing various documents in support of the
case of the petitioner.
4. The respondent no. 2 has filed his counter
affidavit. Shri S.N. Babulkar, learned Advocate General
appearing for the State, submits that the writ petition is
frivolous, malafide and motivated; that there is no
element of public interest involved therein; that a
frivolous petition has been filed which requires to be
rejected outright; that reckless allegations have been
made against the State which are unfounded; that the
writ petition has been filed at the behest of one Shri Anil
Kumar who was an employee of the State Government in
the same department; and that he had earlier filed
WPSB No. 79 of 2016 before this Hon'ble Court wherein
the same set of facts and allegations have been made.
Ultimately, the Hon'ble High Court permitted him to
withdraw the writ petition. Thereafter, the instant
petition is filed. The various documents relied upon in
the said writ petition form part and parcel of this writ
petition. The petitioner has failed to show as to how he
came into possession of the various documents that have
been filed along with the writ petition. For example,
annexure no. 1 is the communication from the Assistant
Commissioner to the Deputy Commissioner. As to how
an inter-departmental communication come to the
possession of the petitioner has not been shown. So also
is with reference to the other documents. Therefore, until
and unless the source of the documents are shown to the
Court, they cannot be relied upon.

4
5. That so far as the allegation regarding failure
of tax collection is concerned the same is belied by the
statistics. The All India Statistics would indicate that the
State of Uttarakhand has been ranked no. 2 when it
comes to tax collection growth for the financial year
2016-2017. On the creation of the State of Uttarakhand,
the tax collection was about Rs. 233 crores. For the
financial year 2016-2017, the tax collection was about
Rs. 7143 crores. This fact itself establishes that the
officers of the department are seriously performing their
duties and are involved in the highest collection of taxes
for the State of Uttarakhand. The writ petition has been
filed with an oblique motive of getting publicity for the
petitioner. Even before the matter was listed before the
Court for consideration, there has been a huge publicity
made in various newspapers. It has been narrated that
there is a tax fraud committed by the State officials. The
names of 12 respondents have been indicated. The good
image and reputation of those respondents have been
tarnished for no reason whatsoever. It is further
submitted that the petitioner himself is a man who has
no respect for law. That he is a tax evader and is liable to
pay a sum of Rs. 6,27,670/- as determined by the tax
department of the State of Uttar Pradesh. He has failed to
remit the tax. Therefore, he himself being a person who
has violated the law cannot espouse the cause of the
public. It is further contended that the petitioner is not a
resident of the State of Uttarakhand as proclaimed by
him. In fact, he is a resident of the State of Uttar
Pradesh. This is a false averment made by the writ
petitioner. One of the pleas of the petitioner was that, in
spite of issuing a show cause notice with regard to the
recovery, the State has not done anything about it. The
same is answered herein that after the show cause notice

5
was issued, necessary actions have been taken against
the concerned officials; that the tax amount has been
recovered and an appropriate action has been initiated
against the concerned officials. The allegation that major
amounts have not been collected by the officers is
opposed to the facts on record of the case. The facts
would indicate that the substantial portions of the
amount due have already been collected by the State. The
amounts, which could not be collected, are presently
under litigation before various forums. Therefore, this
fact clearly indicates that the State of Uttarakhand has
been very vigilant when it comes to dealing with the
discipline of the government officers. The moment the
complaint was received, appropriate and necessary action
has been taken by the State. The documents produced by
the petitioner in the supplementary affidavit clearly
indicate that he is the Treasurer of the Uttar Pradesh,
Vyapar Sangathan. It also indicates his residential
address that he is staying in Meerut. The address is of
the same locality in which Shri Anil Kumar is a resident
of. Therefore, this clearly shows the nexus between the
petitioner and Shri Anil Kumar; that Shri Anil Kumar has
initiated the previous writ petition and is the mastermind
of the present writ petition for obvious reasons. In
February 2014, 33 officers of the Commercial Tax
Department, Uttarakhand submitted a representation
before the Commissioner Commercial Tax, Uttarakhand
making serious allegations against Shri Anil Kumar on
grounds of corruption. Thereafter, Shri Anil Kumar
executed a Mafinama wherein he apologized for the
incident. The said document is marked as annexure
CA-10. The said Shri Anil Kumar has been very active on
social media channels and is regularly making reckless
allegations against the officers of the Government. None

6
of the material is supported by any evidence whatsoever.
Under these circumstances, it is pleaded that none of the
allegations made by the petitioner is supported by any
evidence on record. The petition is hit by malafides. It is
filed with an oblique motive. One of the objects of the
petitioner is to cause loss of reputation to respondent
nos. 9 to 43, and that the same set of facts and figures
were alleged in the earlier WPSB No. 79 of 2016. The
present writ petition is nothing but a similar copy of the
earlier writ petition. Hence, on these grounds, it is
pleaded that the writ petition be dismissed by imposing
heavy costs on the writ petitioner.
6. Shri Rakesh Thapliyal, learned senior counsel
appears on behalf of the counsel representing respondent
no. 12. A counter affidavit has been filed. We have
considered the same. Learned senior counsel submits
that the petition is not maintainable and is liable to be
dismissed; that reckless allegations have been made by
the petitioner against this respondent; that the material
on record would clearly indicate that an identical writ
petition was filed by Shri Anil Kumar being WPSB No. 79
of 2016 and the same was dismissed as withdrawn. The
very same facts have been narrated in the present
petition. The same is also evident from the fact that in
para 29 of the writ petition, the petitioner has stated that
the said Anil Kumar fought against corruption in the
society. It is further contended that there is no proof of
the residential address of the petitioner and he has given
an address situated at Roorkee, State of Uttarakhand.
However, the documents annexed along with the
supplementary affidavit indicate that he is a resident of
Modipuram at Meerut, State of Uttar Pradesh. The
address of the petitioner would indicate that he is the

7
neighbour of the said Anil Kumar. He also contends that
wide publicity was given to the writ petition even before it
was placed for consideration before this Court. He refers
to the various paper publications which indicate that ten
thousand crores is the corruption money which is going
into the personal accounts of the officers of the Tax
Department. Therefore, he pleads that the entire petition
is nothing but a petition for advertisement and cheap
publicity. None of the allegations, as stated by the
petitioner, have been proved. Except for making reckless
allegations, nothing else can be found in the writ petition.
Hence, he pleads that the petition be dismissed with
exemplary cost.
7. Shri B.P. Nautiyal, learned senior counsel
appears on behalf of the counsel representing respondent
no. 15. He submits that the petition is not maintainable.
It is for this reason that the Division Bench of this Court
vide its order dated 19.04.2018, having prima facie found
that the petition is not maintainable, directed the
petitioner to deposit a sum of Rs. 1 lakh with the registry
of the Court. The only object of the petitioner is to create
some sort of advertisement for himself. The petition has
been widely published even before it was listed for
consideration before this Court. He contends that the
petition has been filed with an oblique motive and does
not require any consideration by this Court. The
statement made by the petitioner that on a rough
estimate a sum of rupees more than ten thousand crores
every year was being diverted is a bald and reckless
allegation made by the petitioner. There is no material to
support such an averment. The reading of the pleadings
in the writ petition would indicate that it is not a public
interest litigation and cannot be entertained based on the

8
opinion of the writ petitioner; that none of the allegations
made by the petitioner deserves any recognition and,
since the same is a motivated petition, it requires to be
dismissed with costs.
8. Shri Shashank Pandey, learned counsel
appears for respondent nos. 13, 19, 27 & 31. Counter
affidavits have been filed. We have considered the same.
It is his submission that the entire petition is a
preconceived petition; that there is no merit in the matter
and the earlier petition was dismissed by this Court
which was filed by Shri Anil Kumar, who is the
mastermind of the present petition. There is not a single
allegation made by the petitioner against any one of these
respondents in the entire pleadings. There is a bald
statement made against the officers of the State,
however, the names of these respondents have been
dragged in. The only intention of the petitioner is to
cause the loss of reputation to the respondents. The writ
petition, therefore, being misconceived and mischievous
requires to be dismissed with costs.
9. Shri Abhijay Negi, learned counsel appears for
respondent nos. 33, 35 42, 45 & 46. He adopts the
arguments advanced by the other learned counsels. He
further states that no individual allegation has been
made against any of these respondents and the petition,
being misconceived, requires to be dismissed with cost.
10. Shri Bhupesh Kandpal, learned counsel
appears for respondent nos. 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 16, 17, 18,
25, 26, 28, 29, 32, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 43 & 44. He adopts
the arguments advanced by the other learned counsels
for the respondents. He further submits that the petition
be dismissed with cost.

9
11. Shri Hari Mohan Bhatia, learned counsel
appears for respondent no. 7.
12. Shri Sandeep Tandon, learned counsel appears
for respondent no. 8.
13. Heard learned counsels.
14. During the course of arguments in this case,
on considering the contentions as well as the counter
affidavits filed by the respondents, the learned counsel
for the petitioner was asked as to whether he would still
like to continue to prosecute this matter or not. On
instructions from his client, who is present along with
him, he submits that irrespective of the counter
affidavits, he proposes to argue on merits. Therefore, we
continued to hear him.
15. At the very first instance, it could be seen that
the writ petition was filed on 12.10.2017. There were
office defects. It was listed before the Division Bench for
consideration for the very first time on 01.11.2017. By
the said order, time was granted to cure the defects.
Between the date of filing and the date of the matter
being first listed before the Court, a number of paper
publications were brought about. Various statements
were made in the social media and an impression was
created that almost ten thousand crores have been
siphoned off by the private respondents; that a P.I.L. has
been filed in the High Court which has been accepted by
the Court; that ten thousand crores rupees is going into
the personal accounts of the private respondents. It is,
therefore, that we asked the learned counsel for the
petitioner to justify as to how he could appear for the
petitioner or how he could draft such pleadings and then

10
take them straight to the press. The petitioner contends
that he has not committed any wrong. That statements
were made before the media in support of the pleadings
in the writ petition.
16. On hearing learned counsel, we have no
hesitation to hold that the act of the petitioner and his
counsel is deplorable, to say the least. Petitions are filed
in the Court of law in order to secure justice. Public
interest litigations are filed in the Court of law to ensure
that the interest of the public is served. But what the
petitioner and his counsel have done leaves much to be
desired. Even though a very feeble attempt has been
made by the counsel for the petitioner that he did not
know anything, we cannot accept such a submission. He
is a responsible officer of the Court. He is a learned
member of the Bar. He should very well know that when
a petition is filed, he must be able to stand by the
pleadings. There is not a single allegation made against
any of the respondents, except respondent no. 12,
regarding the financial irregularities. A blanket allegation
has been made and all this is done only to secure
publicity. Rather than pursuing the matter before the
Court of law, the matter was pursued in the newspapers
and the social media. The object is only to cause
humiliation and disrepute not only to the State and its
officials, but also to the private respondents. The act
committed by the petitioner and his counsel cannot be
condoned in any manner.
17. So far as the merits of the case are concerned,
we do not find any ground to entertain this petition at all.
The petition lacks public interest. It is private interest
litigation. It is a litigation initiated to gain cheap publicity
by the petitioner. If the intention of the petitioner was to

11
ensure cleanliness in any department of the government,
the petition should have been filed with verifiable and
relevant statements. There was no need to narrate the
names of the private respondents without even
whispering even a single word about any one of them.
Therefore, the object was only to humiliate them.
18. The counter affidavits filed by various
respondents clearly show that respondents have been
falsely implicated in this petition. They have been
dragged to this Court for no fault of theirs. There is no
question that any one of the respondents was liable to
answer.
19. The plea of the petitioner is ostensibly to bring
to the notice of the Court the large scale corruption that
is going on in the State of Uttarakhand. The same has
been effectively defended by the learned advocate general.
He has placed material on record to indicate the
superiority of the State of Uttarakhand in matters of tax
collection. When the State was collecting tax at about
Rs. 233 crores per annum earlier, for the years 2016-
2017, the tax collection rose to almost Rs. 7143 crores.
This itself shows the manner in which the State has been
employing itself for purposes of tax collection.
20. So far as the show cause notice issued to the
concerned officers is concerned, the learned advocate
general brought it to our notice that an appropriate
action has been initiated against the officers; that sums
due have already been collected. Therefore, to say that
the State is inactive or not performing its duty to ensure
proper collection of taxes or not taking action against
those who were found doing illegal activities is a wrong
statement made by the petitioner. All that is required to
be done by the State has been performed by them.

12
21. Reckless and irresponsible statements have
been made by the petitioner. There is not a single
material produced by him to substantiate his claim.
There is no honesty in the petition. It is a malafide
petition. The writ petition papers in WPSB No. 79 of
2016, when compared with the present petition, clearly
indicate that both the petitions are similar. The
documents produced in this petition have not been
substantiated by the petitioner. There are
communications inter se between the departments of the
State. The petitioner is liable to bring it to the notice of
the Court as to how he got into possession of such
privileged communications. In spite of asking repeated
questions, he has failed to answer. There is no source for
the documents produced by him. The communications
are inter-departmental communications of the officers of
the State. Therefore, this would clearly indicate that all
these material are those material that have been
furnished to the writ petitioner by Shri Anil Kumar,
namely, the writ petitioner in WPSB No. 79 of 2016. It is
also brought to our notice that on charges of corruption,
the said Shri Anil Kumar is presently under custody. The
material would also indicate that the residential address
of the petitioner is next to the residential address of that
of Anil Kumar. Therefore, the nexus between the
petitioner and Shri Anil Kumar has been established.
22. Except against respondent no. 12, there are no
statements or allegations made against any of the other
private respondents. In case, the plea of the petitioner
were to be true, he would have narrated with regard to
the allegations against each one of the private
respondents. He has not done so. Apparently, he cannot

13
do so. He has included the names of all these officers
only to cause disrepute to them. There is virtually
nothing on record to indicate or even an allegation that
any one of these private respondents are guilty of the
allegations made by the petitioner. Therefore, impleading
these respondents and publishing their names in the
media clearly indicates the attitude of the petitioner.
23. The plea of the petitioner is that there has
been a tax evasion of more than ten thousand crores. The
same is belied by the statement of the learned advocate
general who has stated that, for the financial year 2016-
2017, the total tax collection was a sum of Rs. 7143
crores. Therefore, when the tax collection itself is Rs.
7143 crores one fails to imagine as to how there can be a
tax evasion of more than ten thousand crores. This is
also a false submission by the petitioner.
24. Even though strict rules of pleading and
evidence are not applicable to a public interest litigation,
the same requires to be done in an acceptable manner.
Reckless and unfounded allegations cannot form part of
pleadings. Whatever the petitioner states, he must be
capable of proving it. Merely, making statements and
injuring the interest of others is unacceptable. Even
though the Courts have been quite liberal in entertaining
public interest litigations, which do not conform to strict
rules of pleadings or evidence, the same does not mean
that each and every petition unsupported by evidence
requires to be accepted. This is one such ideal case.
Except making allegations, there is no material produced
by the petitioner. There has to be something to accept the
pleading of the petitioner. There is absolutely nothing to
support the petitioner.

14
25. For all these reasons, we have absolutely no
hesitation to hold that this is a coloured writ petition. It
is filed with a malafide intention. There is zero public
interest involved. The petition has been filed for purposes
of obtaining cheap publicity by the petitioner. His object
was also to ensure that loss of reputation accrues to the
private respondents. A public interest litigation cannot be
converted into a litigation for personal gains. Misuse of
the jurisdiction of public interest is rampant in this case.
At the very inception itself, the Court has directed the
petitioner to deposit a cost of Rs. 1 lakh. Therefore, in
view of the manner in which the petition has been drafted
and filed, the reckless and unsubstantiated allegations
made therein, we are of the view that the petitioner
should be saddled with costs. An appropriate message
should be sent, to ensure that the jurisdiction of public
interest litigation, which is intended for the interest of
public at large, is not misused by such kind of writ
petitioners.
26. For all the aforesaid reasons, the writ petition
being devoid of merit, is dismissed. The petitioner is
directed to pay a sum of Rs. 1 lakh with the registry of
this Court within a period of two weeks from today. On
such a deposit being made, the said sum of Rs. 1 lakh as
well as Rs. 1 lakh deposited in terms of the order dated
19.04.2018 is directed to be transferred to the account of
the Uttarakhand High Court Lawyers Welfare Fund.
 (N.S. Dhanik, J.) (Ravi Malimath, ACJ.)
 19.08.2020 AK/SB
